Title: When Chain-of-Thought Fails, the Solution Hides in the Hidden States
Text:
When Chain-of-Thought Fails, the Solution Hides in the Hidden States
Houman Mehrafarin1,2
Amit Parekh1
Ioannis Konstas1
1Heriot-Watt University, Edinburgh, United Kingdom
2University of Edinburgh, Edinburgh, United Kingdom
{h.mehrafarin, amit.parekh, i.konstas}@hw.ac.uk
Abstract
Whether intermediate reasoning is computa-
tionally useful or merely explanatory depends
on whether chain-of-thought (CoT) tokens con-
tain task-relevant information. We present a
mechanistic causal analysis of CoT on GSM8K
using activation patching: transferring token-
level hidden states from a CoT generation to a
direct-answer run for the same question, then
measuring the effect on final-answer accuracy.
Across models, generating after patching yields
substantially higher accuracy than both direct-
answer prompting and the original CoT trace,
revealing that individual CoT tokens can en-
code sufficient information to recover the cor-
rect answer, even when the original trace is in-
correct. This task-relevant information is more
prevalent in correct than incorrect CoT runs
and is unevenly distributed across tokens, con-
centrating in mid-to-late layers and appearing
earlier in the reasoning trace. Moreover, patch-
ing language tokens such as verbs and enti-
ties carry task-solving information that steers
generation toward correct reasoning, whereas
mathematical tokens encode answer-proximal
content that rarely succeeds. Patched outputs
are often shorter and yet exceed the accuracy of
a full CoT trace, suggesting complete reason-
ing chains are not always necessary. Together,
these findings demonstrate that CoT encodes
recoverable, token-level problem-solving infor-
mation, offering new insight into how reason-
ing is represented and where it breaks down.1
1
Introduction
Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting improves per-
formance on multi-step reasoning tasks by eliciting
intermediate reasoning traces before the final an-
swer (Wei et al., 2022; Kojima et al., 2022; Yao
et al., 2023b). On arithmetic benchmarks such
as GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), this consistently

yields higher accuracy than direct-answer prompt-
ing (Wei et al., 2022; Kojima et al., 2022). How-
ever, it remains unclear whether generated CoT
tokens encode information useful for producing the
correct final answer, and whether such information
persists even when the CoT generation itself is in-
correct. Understanding what the CoT hidden states
contain is important for explaining whether inter-
mediate reasoning is computationally useful rather
than merely explanatory (Turpin et al., 2023a; Lan-
ham et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2025), and for under-
standing how reasoning unfolds during inference
(Geva et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023a).
We present a mechanistic analysis of CoT rea-
soning on GSM8K arithmetic problems. We hy-
pothesise that CoT tokens differ in how much task-
relevant information their hidden states encode for
the correct final answer. To test this, we use a
causal intervention framework (Vig et al., 2020;
Meng et al., 2022; Stolfo et al., 2023) that patches
hidden states from individual tokens in a CoT gen-
eration (e.g., “think step-by-step”) into the same
layer of a direct-answer run (e.g., “do not show
steps”) for the same arithmetic problem, measuring
the effect on final-answer accuracy (see Figure 1).
We show that CoT hidden states often encode
sufficient task-relevant information to produce
the correct answer in both LLaMA 3.1 8B and
Qwen 2.5 7B, including where the original CoT is
incorrect. Based on this, we find that correct CoT
generations contain broadly recoverable infor-
mation in their hidden states—such that contin-
uing generation after patching yields the correct
final answer—whereas incorrect generations lack
this property, suggesting reasoning failures occur
because task-relevant information is either absent
or less prevalent across the reasoning trace. Within
these traces, recoverable information concentrates
in mid-to-late layers and earlier positions, and
is unevenly distributed across token roles, with
verb tokens yielding more successful patches than

Patching language
tokens (e.g., verbs and entities) elicit reasoning
that carries information on how to solve the task,
whereas mathematical tokens (e.g., operands, num-
bers) tend to bypass reasoning entirely, producing
the final answer that is rarely correct. Notably,
patching often leads to shorter outputs which
still exceed original CoT accuracy, suggesting a
full CoT reasoning trace is not always necessary
for strong performance. Together, these findings
demonstrate that CoT encodes recoverable, token-
level problem-solving information in its hidden
states, offering a new lens for understanding where
reasoning succeeds, where it breaks down, and how
much of the generated trace is actually necessary.

Related Work
CoT Prompting and Reasoning
CoT prompt-
ing improves performance on multi-step reasoning
benchmarks by encouraging models to generate
intermediate reasoning steps before producing a
final answer (Wei et al., 2022; Kojima et al., 2022).
Subsequent work extends this paradigm through
methods such as self-consistency, which aggregates
answers across sampled reasoning paths (Wang
et al., 2023b; Taubenfeld et al., 2025), and struc-
tured reasoning frameworks that guide or search
over intermediate steps (Yao et al., 2023a; Zelik-
man et al., 2022). Despite these gains, several stud-
ies question whether generated reasoning traces
faithfully reflect the model’s internal computation.
In particular, Turpin et al. (2023b) and Paul et al.
(2024) show that final answers can diverge from
the generated chains, suggesting that key aspects
of the reasoning process may occur independently
of the CoT generated by the model.
Mechanistic and Causal Interpretability
Mech-
anistic interpretability seeks to explain model be-
haviour by identifying internal circuits responsi-
ble for specific outputs (Olah et al., 2020; Elhage
et al., 2021; Conmy et al., 2023; Nanda et al., 2023;
Wang et al., 2023a). Complementary causal ap-
proaches analyse how intermediate representations
contribute to predictions through targeted inter-
ventions such as activation patching (Pearl, 2001;
Geiger et al., 2021; Meng et al., 2022; Zhang and
Nanda, 2024), enabling localisation of representa-
tions that causally influence model outputs.
Interpretability for Reasoning
Recent work ap-
plies these techniques to reasoning tasks: identify-
ing neurons, attention heads, and circuits involved
in arithmetic and symbolic computation (Stolfo
et al., 2023; Yu and Ananiadou, 2024; Brinkmann
et al., 2024; Hou et al., 2023). These studies fur-
ther show how reasoning failures can arise from
incorrect intermediate states and how targeted in-
terventions can help to repair them (Li et al., 2024;
Bertolazzi et al., 2025).
Methodologically,
our work is related to
activation-level probing approaches such as Patch-
scopes (Ghandeharioun et al., 2024), which use
hidden-state interventions to inspect encoded infor-
mation. However, Patchscopes does not analyse
reasoning chains or their causal role in final an-
swers. Closer in objective is Chen et al. (2025),
2


who study CoT using sparse autoencoders and acti-
vation patching to identify latent reasoning features
and transfer them into non-CoT runs. In contrast,
we study the generated CoT tokens, asking which
tokens and positions encode task-relevant infor-
mation and whether these representations causally
contribute to producing the correct final answer.
3
Methodology
3.1
Model & Dataset
We use LLaMA 3.1 8B-Instruct (Grattafiori
et al., 2024) and Qwen 2.5 7B-Instruct (Qwen
et al., 2025) as our base models2 and evaluate
on GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), a multi-step
arithmetic reasoning benchmark containing 1, 319
test examples. We select this dataset for the fol-
lowing reasons: CoT prompting yields substantial
improvements over direct answering (Table 2),
solving each problem requires accumulating
intermediate results through arithmetic operations,
making it well-suited for studying how reasoning
unfolds across token positions.
3.2
Causal Intervention and Task Setup
We compare two zero-shot prompting conditions
for the same question. The source prompt elicits
CoT reasoning, and we cache the residual hidden
states (i.e. the output of each transformer block) at
every layer and token position across the generated
CoT sequence. The target prompt requests only a
final answer, with no CoT reasoning. We intervene
on the target forward pass via activation patching—
at a chosen layer l,3 replacing the hidden state at the
final token position with the cached hidden state of
a specific source CoT token,4 after which the model
continues generating normally. See Appendix A.1
for examples of both prompts.
We use the direct-answer prompt as the target
because it typically fails to solve the task (Table 2),
making it a controlled setting in which improve-
ments after patching can be attributed to informa-
tion transferred from the CoT source representa-
tions. By varying the source CoT token and layer,
this intervention lets us identify where task-relevant

3.3
Token Role Labelling
Each generated source CoT token has semantic
properties that reflect its function in the reasoning
trace. To identify which token types carry task-
relevant information, we assign each source token a
semantic role label and analyse patching success by
group (see Appendix C for implementation details).
The full set of role definitions and examples is

4
Model Performance after Patching
We investigate how task-relevant information is
distributed across CoT hidden states, and whether
targeted patching can recover correct answers even
from incorrect CoT runs. We refer to a source run
as correct if the CoT generation produces the cor-
rect final answer, and incorrect otherwise. Table 2
confirms that while CoT prompting substantially
improves performance on GSM8K—from 8.7%
to 84.6% for LLaMA 3.1 8B and from 19.8% to
89.2% for Qwen 2.5 7B—failure cases persist. As
shown in Table 2, patch accuracy substantially ex-
ceeds both CoT and non-CoT baselines. Notably,

4.1
Availability of Task-Relevant Information
To understand why CoT falls short of near-perfect
accuracy, we examine whether patch success den-
sity differs between correct and incorrect CoT
runs, hypothesising that incorrect examples ex-
hibit sparser encoding of task-relevant information
across tokens and layers than correct ones.
Figure 2 confirms this hypothesis: examples
with correct source CoT runs exhibit substantially
higher patch success density than incorrect ones;
a randomly drawn correct example has an approx-
imately 82% probability of having higher density
than a randomly drawn incorrect example.5 These
results suggest that, although representations suf-
ficient for the correct answer do emerge even in
failing runs, they are neither consistently propa-
gated nor dominant—and in six incorrect-CoT ex-
amples, no intervention recovers the correct answer
at any position or layer, accounting for the residual
0.5% gap in patch accuracy (Table 2). Instead, hid-
den states that steer generation toward incorrect
outputs can dominate, leading to an incorrect fi-
nal answer despite task-relevant signal recoverable
elsewhere in the CoT. Figures 3a and 3b illustrate
this contrast in two representative cases.

4.2
Layer-Wise Information Distribution
We examine whether task-relevant information con-
centrates in particular parts of the model depth.
As individual layer-wise trends can be noisy, we
group layers into Early, Mid, and Late categories
and compute PSR for each group. Table 3 shows
that recoverable task-relevant information is con-
centrated in mid-to-late layers in both models.
For LLaMA 3.1 8B, the peak occurs at layer 17,
whereas for Qwen 2.5 7B, it occurs at the final
layer. This depth-dependent pattern is consistent
with prior work showing that transformer represen-
tations become increasingly task-oriented in later
layers (Zhao et al., 2024).
4.3
Token Role and Patch Success Rate
We examine whether models preferentially encode
task-relevant information within particular token
roles by computing the PSR for each role category.
For example, the CoT phrase “Janet’s ducks lay 16
eggs per day” is assigned the role sequence [step,
step, entity, other, other, verb, other,
quantity, unit, unit].
Table 4 shows that recoverable task-relevant in-
formation is distributed unevenly across token roles.
Semantically informative roles—entity, verb, and
other—yield higher PSR than explicitly mathemat-
ical tokens such as quantities, operands, operators,
and equation-related symbols, with punctuation
contributing the least.6 This pattern suggests that
task-relevant information is often encoded in
broader contextual representations rather than
solely in symbolic mathematical notation. The
strong performance of other, which groups all
tokens not assigned a specific role, suggests that
role labels alone do not fully explain where task-
relevant information concentrates. We therefore
turn to token position as a complementary account.
4.4
Token Position and Patch Success Rate
We hypothesise that the relative position of a to-
ken within the source CoT influences where task-
relevant information is localised. To this end, we
group token positions into quartiles (Q1 earliest,
Q4 latest) and compute the PSR for each.
Table 5 shows that task-relevant information con-
centrates in earlier CoT tokens, with PSR declining
monotonically from Q1 to Q4. This suggests that
the model encodes information most useful for
correct answer prediction in the initial stages of
the reasoning chain, with later tokens primarily
elaborating or verbalising reasoning steps rather
than introducing new task-relevant content.

5
Post-Patch Generation Behaviour
Patching the hidden states of CoT tokens from the
source run into the final position of the target run
can substantially alter the model’s generation be-
haviour. By substituting the hidden state at a single
layer and position, we directly intervene on the rep-
resentation from which the model predicts its next
token, making generation behaviour a natural lens
through which to measure the downstream effect of
this intervention. We analyse this shift in two ways:
by quantifying the causal effect of the intervention,
and by examining the resulting generations.7
5.1
Patch Effect
Following Zhang and Nanda (2024), we measure
the patch effect (PE)—how much the intervention
reduces the probability of the model’s original pre-
diction. For example, if the model assigns probabil-

Figure 4 shows the log PE across entity types

types, which we attribute to the final target posi-

patching (Appendix E). The effect is strongest in
mid-to-late layers, suggesting these layers hold the
representations most effective at redirecting the
model’s output. Numeric entity types—number,
operand, quantity, and result—show a com-
paratively smaller shift, likely because the target
prompt primes the model towards numeric out-
puts, meaning that these patches tend to swap one
number-oriented representation for another.

Prevalence of Final Only does not imply success.
Across all token types, Final Only is the most fre-

pre-conditions the model toward short numeric out-

(62.5%) and Equation Only (51.8%).
Language tokens elicit richer outputs with
higher success rates.
Verb, entity, and other

and Equation Only outputs and attain the highest

elicit Full CoT in 30.4% of interventions with

indicating that language tokens encode sufficient
task-relevant information to derive the correct an-

when patched.
Mathematical tokens encode narrow informa-
tion that does not reliably guide reasoning.
Numeric tokens (result, number, quantity,
operand) concentrate in Final Only outputs (69–

the encoded information and not the output form.
Operator is a partial exception: it produces the
highest Equation Only rate (42.5%) but its PSR
within that form remains below language tokens,
suggesting that its hidden state encodes a local

derive the correct answer.

5.3
Generated Output Length
While patching induces different generation be-
haviours, it is unclear whether the observed ac-
curacy gains require as many tokens as a full CoT
trace. To probe this, we draw hidden states from
disjoint CoT quartiles (Q1: 0–25%, Q2: 25–50%,
etc.) and restrict post-patch generations to one of
four token budgets (25, 50, 150, or 300 tokens), re-
porting patch accuracy under each joint condition
alongside a length-matched no-patch baseline.
Table 8 shows that patching recovers strong
accuracy with substantially fewer tokens than
the source CoT. Every quartile exceeds 94% accu-
racy under a 50-token budget, while the unpatched
source run solves no examples under the same con-
straint. This asymmetry indicates that the CoT
trace is too long to satisfy tight token budgets, but
a single patched hidden state from that trace can
elicit a short, correct generation. Later source po-
sitions outperform earlier ones under the strictest
budget (25 tokens), as Q4 reaches 94.5% compared
to 80.5% for Q1, consistent with later tokens en-
coding more recoverable answer-proximal content
in compact outputs. Once the budget is relaxed
to 50 tokens or more, all quartiles converge above
94%, indicating that task-relevant information
sufficient for correct-answer recovery is broadly
distributed across the reasoning trace.
6
Conclusion
Through causal intervention, we showed that the
CoT generated by a model frequently contains re-
coverable task-solving information—even when
that model ultimately answers incorrectly. This in-
formation is unevenly distributed: correct traces are
denser and more widely accessible, while incorrect
ones are sparser but often still sufficient. Interven-
tions also reshape subsequent generation behaviour,
with patches from certain source tokens produc-
ing much shorter outputs while still surpassing the
model’s original CoT accuracy. Together, these
findings suggest that full natural-language CoT is
neither always necessary nor optimal for represent-
ing task-solving information, and that strong rea-
soning can persist in internal states even when not
fully reflected in the generated chain—motivating
8


future work on making reasoning both more effec-
tive and efficient.
Limitations
Although our framework enables causal analy-
sis of how CoT hidden states contribute to final-
answer prediction, the current study is limited to
the GSM8K arithmetic benchmark. While the pro-
posed intervention method is general and applica-
ble to other multi-step reasoning tasks, evaluating
broader domains remains future work. Recent work
has similarly questioned the efficiency of full CoT
traces: Zhao et al. (2025) find that only a small sub-
set of reasoning steps genuinely drive the model’s
final prediction while the majority are decorative.
Our findings converge on this conclusion from the
hidden-state perspective—task-relevant informa-
tion is unevenly distributed across tokens and lay-
ers, and correct answers are often recoverable from
a small subset of positions.
Our analysis of token entity types relies on a
lightweight labelling procedure combining spaCy
parsing with rule-based heuristics. Because seman-
tic roles in generated CoT are often ambiguous,
some tokens may be misclassified, which may af-
fect fine-grained comparisons across entity cate-
gories.
Our classification of post-patch generation be-
haviour into discrete output types relies on rule-
based criteria applied to surface-level properties
of the generated text. While this scheme captures
the dominant generation patterns observed in prac-
tice, boundaries between categories are not always
sharp. For instance, the distinction between Partial
CoT and Equation Only can be ambiguous when
generations contain minimal but non-zero prose.
Such edge cases may introduce noise into the dis-
tribution statistics reported in §5.2, though they are
unlikely to affect the broader conclusions given
the magnitude of the observed differences across
output types.
Finally, we focus on token-level hidden-state
interventions and do not analyse the latent monose-
mantic features that may underlie these represen-
tations. Understanding how such internal features
relate to the recoverable task-relevant information
identified in this study remains an important direc-
tion for future work.

C
Token Role Labelling
We assign a single role to each token in the Chain-
of-Thought trace using a deterministic rule-based
pipeline. At a high level, the labeller first extracts
salient nouns and proper nouns from the question
and uses them to mark related mentions in the rea-
soning trace as ENTITY, including some co-referent
pronouns. It then identifies verbs, numbers, units,
and quantities using part-of-speech tags and depen-
dency relations. Arithmetic structure is labelled
separately: numbers that participate in equations
are tagged as OPERAND or RESULT, while symbolic
and textual operators (e.g., +, −, ×) are tagged
as OPERATOR, and equality symbols are tagged as
EQUALS. The pipeline also marks explicit reasoning-
step indicators such as Step 1: as STEP, assigns
stand-alone punctuation to PUNCT, and uses OTHER
as a fallback category for tokens not captured by
the preceding rules. When multiple rules apply to
the same token, a fixed priority ordering resolves
the conflict so that arithmetic and structural roles
override more general semantic labels.

To verify that the difference in patch success den-

Whitney U (MWU) test. We chose this test for
two reasons: firstly, the patch success density is
bounded between 0–100% and exhibits a right-
skewed distribution, particularly in the wrong con-
dition (mean = 12.57, median = 8.10); and sec-
ondly, our groups are unequal in size (n = 1,108
vs. n = 211), thereby making rank-based compari-
son more appropriate.

Abstract: Whether intermediate reasoning is computa- tionally useful or merely explanatory depends on whether chain-of-thought (CoT) tokens con- tain task-relevant information. We present a mechanistic causal analysis of CoT on GSM8K using activation patching: transferring token- level hidden states from a CoT generation to a direct-answer run for the same question, then measuring the effect on final-answer accuracy. Across models, generating after patching yields substantially higher accuracy than both direct- answer prompting and the original CoT trace, revealing that individual CoT tokens can en- code sufficient information to recover the cor- rect answer, even when the original trace is in- correct. This task-relevant information is more prevalent in correct than incorrect CoT runs and is unevenly distributed across tokens, con- centrating in mid-to-late layers and appearing earlier in the reasoning trace. Moreover, patch- ing language tokens such as verbs and enti- ties carry task-solving information that steers generation toward correct reasoning, whereas mathematical tokens encode answer-proximal content that rarely succeeds. Patched outputs are often shorter and yet exceed the accuracy of a full CoT trace, suggesting complete reason- ing chains are not always necessary. Together, these findings demonstrate that CoT encodes recoverable, token-level problem-solving infor- mation, offering new insight into how reason- ing is represented and where it breaks down.1
